ui.answer: Yes for the defects found: a component-test layer (sfdx-lwc-jest in Node, no org) would have caught the chess play() race, both runs' surviving LWC mutants, the Battleship races before Improve did, and the unlabeled buttons. Headless Chromium on a local page adds real accessibility-tree, console and layout checks but costs a build for LWC. Only an on-target check (a person, or a harness-held session) or a read-only visibility query catches the hidden tab. Neither run used any of these: the stand-in probe proved Chrome starts, then both strategies excluded Jest with the reason that it is not the org.

planning.answer: Planning made the model plan one suite, the org Apex suite, plus source greps and a manual browser procedure. It did not plan test layers per concern with an executable command each. The Apex rules were planned thoroughly (22 chess cases with exact FENs; 10 Battleship procedures). The UI concern had no executable layer in either run, and test-spec's focused-only rule left 7 of 10 Battleship methods without a case.

The gate checks structure only: every UI or interactive requirement has a component or rendered-local row with a command, or a reason naming what blocks it.
